title: Seed stitch cot blanket
subtitle: A flat-lying cot blanket in DK seed stitch, worked as a single panel.
excerpt: A 75 by 90 cm cot blanket worked flat in seed stitch (US: moss stitch) on 4 mm needles. Seed stitch does not curl at the edges, making it a practical all-over pattern for a baby blanket that needs no border and no blocking to lie flat.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 5th series (1889), §Knitted Toilet Covers and Baby Wraps, cites seed stitch and moss stitch as standard flat-lying fabric patterns for nursery use. Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), §Baby Wraps, recommends alternating knit and purl stitches across a baby blanket for the same reason: no curling at the edges.

glossaryTerms.definition: A reversible fabric made by alternating knit and purl stitches across each row and then reversing them on the next row, so a knit sits on top of a purl and a purl sits on top of a knit. Called seed stitch in the US and moss stitch in the UK; both produce the same pebbly texture. Lies flat without curling.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat in
seed stitch
(UK: moss stitch) on 4 mm needles, finishing at 75 cm wide by 90 cm long.

A single panel keeps seam count to zero, which matters for a blanket that will go through the washing machine regularly. Seed stitch was chosen over plain garter stitch for its texture: the alternating knit-purl pebbly surface gives the fabric more visual interest than ridged garter without any additional technique. Like garter stitch, seed stitch lies flat on both sides, so no border or blocking is needed to keep the corners from curling. Budget about 255 g (about 560 m / 615 yards) of machine-washable DK. Buy all the yarn at once in matched dye lots. A blanket this size typically draws from two or three skeins, and a dye-lot shift mid-row is visible against seed stitch's textured surface. Drape across a cot or fold for a pram bag.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 255 g (about 560 m / 615 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn
items.substitutions: Superwash merino DK or DK wool-cotton blend. Cotton DK works but is heavier and denser at this gauge; allow an extra 30 g and check finished dimensions. Non-superwash wool felts in the machine wash.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 40 rows to 10 cm over seed stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked. Seed stitch produces a slightly longer row than garter stitch at the same needle size because the purl bumps push the rows apart less. Work a 15 cm square swatch in seed stitch, leave it flat overnight, and measure the centre 10 cm. Do not measure immediately off the needles: the fabric relaxes slightly over the first few minutes.

If your gauge is 20 stitches per 10 cm, the blanket will come out about 82 cm wide instead of 75 cm at a 165-stitch cast-on. If your gauge is 24 stitches per 10 cm, the width will be about 69 cm. The row gauge matters too: at 38 rows per 10 cm instead of 40, the blanket will be about 4 cm shorter at the same row count. Measure in both directions and adjust needle size.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 165 stitches. An odd stitch count makes seed stitch simpler: Row 1 begins k1, and because the row ends on k1, Row 2 also begins k1, and the pattern alternates naturally from there.

Long-tail tail length: (4 mm × 165) / 10 + 15 = 81 cm. Measure out 90 cm of tail before starting; round up to 110 cm to leave a comfortable margin. A blanket cast-on is long enough that running out of tail partway through forces an unravelling and restart.
Body
Every row (RS and WS): *k1, p1; repeat from * to last stitch, k1.

Because the stitch count is odd (165), the pattern starts and ends with k1 on every row. The purl and knit stitches align in a checkerboard over the rows, producing the characteristic pebbly texture. There is no separate right-side row or wrong-side row to track.

Work until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on edge. At gauge that is 360 rows, but measure rather than count. When you set this aside between sessions, jot the row number or place a marker; the pattern is easy to pick up mid-row because the stitch you need to work next is always the opposite of what is showing on the needle tip.
Stitch count check-ins

At row 180 (halfway, about 45 cm): count the stitches on the needle. You should have 165. If the count has risen by one or two, scan back along the last few rows for a bar of yarn that has been knitted rather than slipped past. Seed stitch makes accidental yarn-overs more visible than stocking stitch, so a drift of even one stitch is usually findable.
At row 358 (two rows before cast-off, about 89.5 cm): count again. If you have 165 stitches, cast off on the following row.
Common faults

Pattern reverting to ribbing: seed stitch requires the stitches to be worked as the opposite of what faces you on the needle, but ribbing works them the same as what faces you. If the fabric begins to look like columns of knit and purl rather than a checkerboard, you have started treating it as ribbing. Check the facing stitch on the needle: if you see a knit, work a purl; if you see a purl, work a knit.

Stitch count drifting up: a yarn-over was worked accidentally before a purl stitch because the yarn was left in front when moving to the knit. After every purl stitch, move the yarn to the back before the next knit. After every knit stitch, move the yarn to the front before the next purl.

Tension loose or uneven at the purl stitches: purl tension is looser for many knitters than knit tension. Work each purl a little more firmly than feels natural, or try a smaller needle if the purl stitches are visibly larger than the knit stitches on the surface of the fabric.
Cast-off

Cast off in pattern: work each stitch as it presents (k the knits, p the purls), passing each stitch over the previous one. A cast-off worked in pattern lies flat and matches the texture of the fabric body.
Finishing

Weave in both ends on the wrong side with the tapestry needle, running each tail at least 5 cm along a row of seed stitch and changing direction once. Trim. Seed stitch lies flat without blocking, but a gentle wash and flat dry will even out any uneven tension areas.
Care

Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle if the yarn label permits. Superwash merino DK tolerates this well. Lay flat to dry; do not tumble dry. The fabric will look slightly puckered straight from the machine but relaxes and smooths as it dries flat.
What to try next

From seed stitch, the natural progression is double moss stitch: a four-row repeat that groups the knit and purl stitches in pairs and produces a larger-scale textured block. The same 165-stitch cast-on and 4 mm needles work for a double-moss cot blanket, and the stitch pattern repeats every 4 rows instead of every 2.
